solution: Fix a target length T and write a_i = q*T + r. Each operation at most doubles the number of pieces, and a leftover piece must survive whenever r > 0 or q > 2^k, so after k operations a carrot yields at most min(q, 2^k - 1) pieces of length T, and q pieces when r = 0 and q <= 2^k; the bound is met for every carrot at once by the single schedule x = 2^(k-1)*T, 2^(k-2)*T, ..., T applied to all carrots, since equal-length pieces are always cut together. Hence answer(k) = max over T of the sum of that per-carrot yield. Once 2^k - 1 >= m the cap never binds and the answer is fixed at the total length (all pieces of length 1), so only O(log m) values of k need real work; each of those is evaluated for every T by sweeping the multiples of T over a prefix-summed value histogram, about O(m log m) per k. The formula matches all six sample outputs exactly and agrees with an exhaustive brute force over cutting schedules on 300 random small inputs.
annotator: claude agent, verified against a brute force
notes: Genuinely different from B1: the hard version turns on the doubling bound min(floor(a_i/T), 2^k - 1) and on the answer saturating at the total length once k >= log2(m), neither of which exists at k = 1. Two techniques here have no slug in the vocabulary: (a) the 'each operation at most doubles the pieces, so 2^k - 1' argument, and (b) the harmonic sweep over multiples of T used to evaluate sum of min(floor(a_i/T), C) for all T; divisor-enumeration and sieve are the nearest labels but both mean something else in this corpus (listing divisors of a number, and prime sieves), so I left them off rather than pollute two small clean labels. 'greedy' is listed at low confidence for the halving cut schedule that attains the bound. Rating is None (contest too new); index B2 reads ~1600-1800.
